chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al-Halby, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he was asked

About a man who passes on a road from the roads of the Muslims, so his animal hits a person with its leg. He (peace be upon him) said: There is no liability upon him for what it hit with its leg, but there is liability upon him for what it hit with its hand, because its leg is behind him if he is riding, and if he was guiding it, then he controls its hand by the Permission of Allah, placing it wherever he wishes.

He said: And he was asked about a camel that was in heat, so it went out from the house and killed a man. So the brother of the man came and struck the stallion with the sword and slew it. He (peace be upon him) said: The owner of the camel is responsible for the blood money, and he takes the price of his camel.
And about a man who causes a man to flee, so he slays him, and his animal slays another man. He (peace be upon him) said: He is responsible for whatever was from something.

key_terms.دَابَّة: Animal (specifically a beast of burden or livestock)
key_terms.دِيَة: Blood money / compensation for death or injury

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on an animal hitting a person on the road?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the principles of *daman* (liability) by distinguishing between natural, involuntary actions of an animal, such as a hind leg kicking while walking, which incur no liability, and controlled actions, like a front leg striking by the owner's will, which do. It further clarifies complex scenarios involving escaped animals (*bukhtiy*) and mutual injury, establishing that the owner remains liable for blood money (*diyah*) while retaining the right to recover the animal's value, reflecting the Shia juristic emphasis on intent and control in civil liability.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Ibn Abu Umeyr, from Hammad, from Al Halby,

(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> having been asked about the man who passes upon a road from the roads of the Muslim, so his animal hits a human being by its (hind) legs. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘There is nothing upon him what it hit by its (hind) legs, but upon him is what it hits by its hands (front legs), because its (hind) legs are behind him if he is riding, and if he was guiding it, so he was in control of its hands (front legs), by the Permission of Allah<sup>azwj</sup>, to place these wherever he so wishes to’.

He (the narrator) said, ‘And he<sup>asws</sup> was asked about a camel in heat, so it went out from the house and killed a man. So a brother of the man came and struck the stallion with the sword and he slew it. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘The owner of the camel is responsible of the wergild and would seize the price of his camel’.
And about the man who caused the man to flee, so another man slew him and his animal. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘He is responsible for whatever was from something’.
